column1: .NET SDK~Build and inspect managed .NET projects and assemblies.~Run `dotnet --info` and `dotnet new console -o Demo`; use `dotnet build` inside a project.~Create a console project, set Program.cs to print `Convert.FromBase64String("ZmxhZw==")` as UTF-8, then `dotnet run`; output is `flag`.~The SDK executes build scripts and package restore can use the network; inspect untrusted projects before building.

7-Zip (7z)~List, test, and extract many archive formats.~Use `7z l archive.zip`, `7z t archive.zip`, and `7z x archive.zip -oout`.~Run `7z l puzzle.zip` to see member names, then `7z x puzzle.zip -oextracted`; inspect an extracted `note.txt` separately.~Extraction can overwrite files or traverse paths; use an empty output directory and inspect listings first.

aircrack-ng~Analyze captured Wi-Fi handshakes and test candidate passphrases in authorized labs.~Start with `aircrack-ng --help`; typical offline form is `aircrack-ng -w words.txt capture.cap`.~Given a competition-provided WPA handshake capture and small supplied wordlist, run the offline check and verify a reported key by reusing it in the lab setup.~A PCAP without a complete relevant handshake cannot validate a password; do not capture or attack unrelated networks.

ALEAPP (Android Logs Events And Protobuf Parser)~Parse Android forensic extractions into artifact reports.~Launch `aleapp` for the GUI or `aleapp --help` for installed CLI syntax.~Add a supplied Android extraction, select an output folder, run parsing, then inspect report entries for a suspicious app message and its source path.~Artifacts depend on Android/app versions; a parsed timestamp needs timezone and source verification.

Android Studio~Inspect and develop Android applications, APK projects, and emulator-based tests.~Open a project or APK; use Logcat and Device Manager for authorized test devices.~Open a provided APK with APK Analyzer, inspect manifest permissions and bundled assets, then compare with jadx's decompiled code.~Building/running an APK executes code; inspect statically first and use an isolated emulator.

angr~Symbolically execute native binaries to solve path constraints.~In Python, start with `import angr; p=angr.Project("chall", auto_load_libs=False)` and use SimulationManager.~For a tiny binary with success/fail print paths, use `simgr.explore(find=success_addr, avoid=failure_addr)` and inspect the found stdin bytes.~Symbolic execution can explode in state count; addresses, input modeling, and external calls must be correct.

AperiSolve~Web-based image steganography analysis service.~Open the permitted AperiSolve instance and upload only a challenge image allowed by event rules.~Upload a supplied PNG, compare bit-plane and metadata results, then independently verify an apparent payload with zsteg or HxD.~An upload sends the file to a third party; never upload private evidence without authorization, and treat automated hits as leads.

Apktool~Decode Android APK resources/smali and rebuild modified copies.~Use `apktool d app.apk -o decoded` and `apktool b decoded -o rebuilt.apk`.~Decode a challenge APK, read `AndroidManifest.xml` and search smali for a hard-coded URL; verify the same URL in JADX.~Rebuilt APKs need signing before installation; resource decoding is not equivalent to decompiling original Java source.

asar (@electron/asar)~List and extract Electron ASAR application bundles.~Use `asar list app.asar` and `asar extract app.asar extracted` (or `npx asar` when packaged that way).~List a supplied `app.asar`, extract it, and inspect `package.json` and JavaScript for a local validation constant.~ASAR is an archive, not encryption; extracted scripts may still be minified or obfuscated.

Audacity~Inspect audio visually and spectrally, and edit copies.~Open audio; switch a track to Spectrogram and use Plot Spectrum for tonal clues.~Open `mystery.wav`, view its spectrogram, and read letters drawn as frequency bands; confirm by replaying/cropping a copy.~Lossy conversion can erase hidden frequencies; preserve the original and note sample rate.

AutoIt-Ripper~Extract scripts and resources from compiled AutoIt executables.~Run the installed tool's `--help` and provide a copied AutoIt PE file.~Extract a challenge executable, inspect recovered script text for a decryption key, and cross-check it against runtime behavior.~Extraction can fail on protected/newer formats; a recovered script may be incomplete.

BinDiff~Compare functions between two binary versions using disassembler databases.~Import both versions into supported disassemblers and run a BinDiff comparison.~Compare original and patched challenge binaries; inspect the one changed function and its control-flow difference.~Function matches are heuristic; verify changes in assembly and bytes.

bkcrack~Recover ZIP traditional-encryption keys from known plaintext.~Use `bkcrack -h` and provide encrypted ZIP plus a known plaintext file/bytes as documented.~If an encrypted ZIP contains a known PNG header, use that known plaintext at the correct offset to recover keys, then test extraction on a copy.~It targets legacy ZipCrypto, not AES ZIP; incorrect plaintext or offset invalidates the attack.

bulk_extractor~Scan disk images/files for features such as emails, URLs, and card-like strings without filesystem parsing.~Run `bulk_extractor -o bulk_out image.dd` on a copied image.~Inspect `email.txt` and `url.txt` in the output to locate a suspicious address, then confirm the byte offset with xxd.~Feature hits can be false positives or stale deleted data; correlate with filesystem context.

bvi~Edit binary files in a vi-like terminal interface.~Open a copy with `bvi file.bin` and use its help for hex editing keys.~Open a copied file, navigate to offset 0, inspect its magic bytes, change one known corrupt byte, save under a new name, and verify with xxd.~Editing the original changes evidence; insert versus overwrite behavior matters.

Bytecode Viewer~Inspect Java class/JAR bytecode and decompiler output through a GUI.~Open the supplied JAR or class and compare decompiler views.~Open a challenge JAR, find its main class, inspect a Base64 constant in decompiled code, then verify it in raw bytecode.~Decompilers can disagree or fail on obfuscation; bytecode is authoritative.

bzip2~Compress/decompress bzip2 streams.~Use `bzip2 -tv file.bz2` to test and `bzip2 -dk file.bz2` to keep the original.~A file starting `BZh` tests cleanly; decompress it and inspect the new file's magic bytes.~Decompression can overwrite similarly named files; use a working copy.

cabextract~List and extract Microsoft CAB archives.~Use `cabextract -l file.cab` and `cabextract -d out file.cab`.~List a supplied CAB, extract into an empty directory, and inspect a recovered DLL or text file.~A CAB may contain nested cabinets or paths; inspect names and extraction output.

capa~Detect capabilities in programs from code patterns and rules.~Run `capa sample.exe` and inspect `capa --help` for output formats.~Run capa on a challenge PE and see “decode data using XOR”; locate the matched function in Ghidra and confirm the loop.~Rules are heuristic and can miss packed code or overstate behavior; inspect the matched code.

Chainsaw~Hunt Windows event logs using Sigma rules and other patterns.~Use `chainsaw --help`; a common action is `chainsaw hunt logs/ -s sigma/ -o results.csv`.~Hunt a supplied EVTX directory, inspect a matching PowerShell event, then open the original log entry to verify fields.~Rule matches are leads, not proof; Sigma fields and mappings vary by rule pack/version.

checksec~Report binary mitigations such as NX, PIE, RELRO, and canaries.~Run `checksec --file=./chall` or your installed build's equivalent.~Check an ELF and note `PIE enabled` and `NX enabled`; account for randomized addresses and non-executable stack in your analysis.~Mitigation reports are properties, not exploitability verdicts; verify architecture and runtime.

crypto-attacks~Collection of cryptanalytic scripts, often Sage/Python, for CTF puzzles.~Read the local README and select a script matching the known weakness.~For an RSA challenge with known `n`, `e`, and ciphertext, choose the specific low-exponent or shared-factor script only after checking its assumptions.~There is no single universal command; scripts may require SageMath and exact input formatting.

curl~Send HTTP requests and inspect responses from the terminal.~Use `curl -i https://target/`, `curl -sS -o page.html URL`, or `curl -X POST -d 'x=1' URL`.~Request a challenge endpoint with `curl -i`, record status/headers, then alter one parameter and compare responses.~Shell quoting, redirects, cookies, and TLS options affect results; use only competition targets.

Cutter~GUI reverse engineering built on Rizin/radare2 ecosystem.~Open a binary, run analysis, inspect Functions, Graph, Strings, and Decompiler panes.~Open a PE, follow a “Correct” string reference to a validation function, and inspect the branch in disassembly.~Decompiler output is approximate; verify with instructions and target architecture.

DB Browser for SQLite~Inspect and edit SQLite databases through a GUI.~Open a copy; use Browse Data, Database Structure, and Execute SQL.~Open `app.db`, list tables, then query `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10;` to inspect challenge records.~Opening writable databases can alter journal state; keep a forensic copy and check WAL files.

DBeaver Community Edition~GUI SQL client for many database engines.~Create a connection to the supplied lab database, inspect schema, then run read-only queries.~Connect to a competition PostgreSQL service, list tables, and query `SELECT count(*) FROM messages;` before drilling into rows.~Drivers may download; credentials and queries can touch a live service, so use organizer-provided scope.

Detect It Easy (DIE)~Identify executable formats, compilers, packers, and protections.~Open a copied binary in the GUI or use installed `diec` CLI if available.~DIE reports UPX on `chall.exe`; confirm with UPX's test command and inspect the unpacked copy in Ghidra.~Signatures are heuristic; a packer label alone does not prove content or safety.

dex2jar~Convert Android DEX bytecode to Java JAR for inspection.~Use `d2j-dex2jar classes.dex -o classes.jar` or installed script variant.~Extract `classes.dex` from an APK, convert it, and open the JAR in Bytecode Viewer to inspect a validator.~Conversion is lossy for some features/obfuscation; JADX or smali may be clearer.

Didier Stevens Beta tools (onedump.py)~Inspect and extract OLE or related embedded data with a beta script.~Use `python onedump.py -h` from the local tool directory to identify options.~Run the script against a supplied Office container, list streams, and extract a suspicious stream to a separate file for inspection.~Beta flags can change; select stream IDs from actual output and preserve the original.

Didier Stevens Suite (pdfid.py, pdf-parser.py, oledump.py and   others)~Analyze PDF, OLE, and document structures with focused Python scripts.~Use `python pdfid.py suspicious.pdf`; then `python pdf-parser.py -h` or `python oledump.py -h`.~Run pdfid to count `/JavaScript` and `/OpenAction` tokens, then use pdf-parser to inspect the referenced object rather than assuming it executes.~Token counts can be hidden/obfuscated or benign; parser versions and script names vary.

Docker Engine and Compose plugin~Run isolated containers and multi-service lab stacks.~Use `docker version`, `docker compose version`, and `docker compose up` in a trusted challenge project.~Start an organizer-provided local web challenge with `docker compose up -d`, then inspect `docker compose ps` and logs before connecting.~Compose files can mount host paths, expose ports, and run arbitrary images; inspect before starting.

dwarf2json~Generate Volatility 3 symbol JSON from DWARF and kernel debug files.~Run `dwarf2json --help` and select Linux/macOS generation mode matching source symbols.~Given a Linux kernel debug ELF and System.map, generate a symbol JSON and place it in Volatility's symbol path; rerun `linux.pslist`.~Kernel build mismatch makes symbols unusable; architecture and debug data must match the memory image.

Eclipse Temurin JDK (OpenJDK)~Run and compile Java programs and JAR-based tools.~Use `java -version`, `javac -version`, `java -jar app.jar`.~Compile `Hello.java` with `javac Hello.java` and run `java Hello`; for a challenge JAR, inspect first, then run only in an isolated lab.~Running a JAR executes its code; Java version compatibility matters.

ewf-tools (libewf)~Read EWF/E01 forensic disk images and expose raw content.~Use `ewfinfo evidence.E01`, `ewfverify evidence.E01`, and `ewfexport evidence.E01` or `ewfmount` with local help.~Verify a provided E01 image, export a raw copy, and pass it to The Sleuth Kit/Autopsy.~E01 segments must be complete; exported data can be very large.

Exploit-DB / searchsploit (offline archive)~Search a local archive of published exploits and advisories.~Use `searchsploit product version` and `searchsploit -x ID` to view an entry.~Search the exact version of a lab service, read a matching advisory locally, then verify prerequisites against the service before any test.~Search results may be stale or inapplicable; an exploit title is not proof of vulnerability.

factordb-python~Query FactorDB for known integer factorizations through a Python client.~Inspect local module help/README and use its FactorDB API with an integer `n`.~For a small CTF RSA modulus, query whether `n` already has known factors and verify their product equals `n` before computing a key.~An online query sends the modulus to a third party and may violate offline rules; use only if permitted.

FakeNet-NG~Simulate network services and capture attempted connections from a sample in a lab.~Run `fakenet --help` or launch its configured GUI/service in an isolated VM.~Start FakeNet in a lab, run a supplied sample, and inspect logs for DNS/HTTP hosts it attempts to contact.~The sample still executes; isolation and network routing must be configured correctly.

Fernflower~Decompile Java class/JAR bytecode to Java-like source.~Run the installed Fernflower JAR with its documented syntax, usually `java -jar fernflower.jar input.jar output_dir`.~Decompile a challenge JAR and inspect a string transformation in the resulting Java files, then compare with raw bytecode.~Decompiled Java is approximate and can misrepresent obfuscated control flow.

Feroxbuster~Discover web paths recursively in an authorized target.~Use `feroxbuster -u http://target/ -w paths.txt` and inspect `--help` for rate/recursion limits.~Against a supplied local web challenge, scan a small wordlist and manually verify a reported `/backup/` path with curl.~Recursive scans can generate heavy traffic; constrain scope, rate, and target.

FFmpeg~Inspect, convert, extract, and filter audio/video streams.~Use `ffmpeg -i media.mp4` for stream info and `ffmpeg -i media.mp4 frame_%04d.png` for frames.~Extract all frames from a supplied video and inspect a one-frame QR code with ZBar; use `ffmpeg -i media.mp4 -vn audio.wav` for audio.~Transcoding is lossy unless configured; keep original and extract without conversion when possible.

ffuf~Fuzz web paths, parameters, or headers against an authorized HTTP target.~Use `ffuf -u http://target/FUZZ -w paths.txt`; inspect `-h` for filters and rate limits.~Scan a local challenge with three candidate paths, compare status/size, and verify a hit with curl.~A 200 response can be a catch-all page; filter by size/content and limit traffic.

file (libmagic)~Identify file formats from signatures and heuristics.~Run `file sample.bin` and `file -k sample.bin` for multiple matches.~A file named `photo.jpg` reports “PDF document”; inspect its first bytes with xxd and use PDF tools.~Heuristics can misidentify polyglots and corrupted files; verify magic and parser behavior.

FLOSS (FLARE Obfuscated String Solver)~Recover static and certain decoded/stack strings from binaries.~Run `floss sample.exe` and inspect `floss -h` for filtering.~FLOSS reports a decoded URL not seen by strings; trace the referenced function in Ghidra and confirm the decode logic.~It may miss custom obfuscation or emit false positives; output is not proof of execution.

foremost~Carve files from raw images by signature.~Use `foremost -i disk.img -o carved_out` and inspect its audit file.~Carve a supplied image, inspect recovered PNG files, then compare offsets with filesystem metadata.~Carving can yield fragmented/partial files and duplicates; an extracted file may lack original path.

FQLite~Recover SQLite records, including deleted/free-list remnants, through a GUI or Java tool.~Open a copy of the SQLite database and inspect recovered tables/records.~A normal query omits a deleted chat row; FQLite recovers a candidate row, which you validate against page bytes and timestamps.~Deleted record recovery is best-effort; WAL and page reuse affect results.

Frida~Instrument running programs by injecting JavaScript hooks in an authorized lab.~Use `frida-ps -U` for a connected device or `frida -f ./app -l hook.js` for a local program, matching platform setup.~Hook a local challenge's comparison function, print its arguments, and verify the observed bytes with static analysis.~Hooks alter timing/behavior and execute target code; attach only to your own lab process.

GCC, G++ and build tools (build-essential, make, CMake,   pkg-config)~Compile C/C++ code and build challenge helpers.~Use `gcc -Wall -O0 demo.c -o demo`, `g++ demo.cpp -o demo`, `make`, or `cmake -S . -B build`.~Compile a tiny parser for a custom binary record and compare its output with Python's struct unpacking.~Makefiles/CMake scripts can execute arbitrary commands; inspect supplied build files first.

GEF (GDB Enhanced Features)~Add reverse-engineering views and commands to GDB.~Start `gdb ./chall`, run `gef help`, and use GEF's context and checksec commands.~Break at main; GEF's context shows registers, stack, and nearby instructions as the program reads input.~GEF requires compatible GDB/Python; commands may differ by installed revision.

Git~Track changes and inspect repository history.~Use `git status`, `git log --oneline --all`, `git show COMMIT:path`, and `git diff`.~In a supplied repository, inspect `git log --all` and find a deleted config file in an earlier commit with `git show`.~History may include secrets; do not push or publish it. Work on a copy before resets or checkouts.

Gitleaks~Scan repositories and files for likely secrets.~Run `gitleaks detect --source .` or installed version's `git`/`dir` subcommand; check `gitleaks --help`.~Scan a provided Git repo; a finding points to a token-like string in a commit, which you inspect via `git show`.~Matches can be false positives; scanning history can expose private secrets in reports.

G'MIC (gmic)~Apply image filters and transforms through a powerful CLI.~Run `gmic -h` and load an image with `gmic image.png ... output result.png`.~Use a contrast/threshold filter on a copied faint image to reveal hidden lettering, then compare with original pixels.~Filter syntax is version-specific and transforms can destroy steganographic bits; keep originals.

GNU Wget~Download files and mirror permitted web content.~Use `wget -O page.html URL` or `wget --spider URL` to test retrieval.~Fetch a challenge-hosted text file to a known path and compare its SHA-256 with the provided checksum.~Recursive mirroring can fetch much more than intended; restrict target and depth.

Go~Build and run Go programs.~Use `go version`, `go run main.go`, and `go build -o app .`.~Write a tiny parser for a length-prefixed message, run it on provided bytes, and verify field lengths against xxd.~Go modules may download dependencies; inspect `go.mod` and source before running.

Gobuster~Discover HTTP paths, DNS names, or virtual hosts using wordlists.~Use `gobuster dir -u http://target/ -w words.txt`; inspect `gobuster --help`.~Against a local lab site, a small list finds `/admin`; verify the response with curl and distinguish it from catch-all 200 pages.~Limit concurrency and scope; DNS/vhost modes need different options and interpretation.

GoReSym~Recover Go symbols, types, and build information from stripped binaries.~Use `GoReSym -h` and run it against a copied Go executable.~Recover function names from a stripped Go challenge, then import or label those names in Ghidra to trace validation.~Packed or corrupted binaries may yield partial data; recovered names need code verification.

GTFOBins (offline copy)~Look up documented behavior of Unix binaries that can matter in a lab privilege scenario.~Search the local HTML/Markdown copy for a specific available binary and scenario.~In an organizer-provided sandbox, check whether a permitted binary has a documented file-read mode, then test only within that sandbox.~Entries are conditional on version, permissions, and configuration; an offline recipe is not a guarantee.

gzip~Compress/decompress gzip streams.~Use `gzip -t file.gz`, `gzip -dk file.gz`, or `gzip -dc file.gz > out.bin`.~A file starts `1f 8b`; test it, decompress to a copy, and inspect the next layer with file/xxd.~Output can overwrite a same-named file; gzip can contain concatenated members.

HackTricks (offline copy)~Search a local knowledge base of security techniques and reference commands.~Use ripgrep against the copied Markdown/HTML: `rg -i 'topic' /path/to/HackTricks`.~Find notes for a specific challenge protocol, check the version assumptions, and test a single hypothesis against the lab.~Reference pages may be stale, broad, or inapplicable; verify primary behavior.

hashcat~Test candidate passwords against supported hash formats using CPU/GPU.~Use `hashcat --help`, `hashcat --example-hashes`, and `hashcat -m MODE -a 0 hashes.txt words.txt`.~Identify a provided hash type, run a small wordlist in the correct mode, and confirm a reported plaintext by rehashing it.~Wrong mode may produce misleading behavior; optimize only after identifying format and salt.

hashid~Guess possible hash types from digest shape.~Run `hashid '5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592'`.~It suggests MD5 among other 32-hex formats; verify using context or known test values before choosing hashcat mode.~Length and alphabet do not uniquely identify a hash.

Hayabusa~Analyze Windows EVTX logs with built-in detection rules and timeline output.~Run `hayabusa --help` and use the timeline command for a supplied log directory.~Generate a timeline from challenge EVTX files, inspect a suspicious logon event, then cross-check the original event fields.~Rule packs/versions affect findings; timestamps need timezone normalization.

hcxtools~Convert and inspect Wi-Fi capture formats used in authorized password auditing.~Use `hcxpcapngtool -h` and inspect a provided capture's output options.~Convert a supplied handshake capture to a hashcat-compatible file, then test only the provided small candidate list.~Conversion output is not proof a valid handshake exists; wireless capture and cracking must stay within contest scope.

Hindsight (pyhindsight)~Parse browser history and related artifacts into a timeline.~Run `hindsight.py --help` or GUI and point it at a copied browser profile.~Parse a provided Chrome profile and find a download URL near the challenge's event time; confirm against SQLite source records.~Browser profiles may be locked or have WAL files; preserve all related files and timezones.

hlextend~Demonstrate hash length-extension attacks against vulnerable prefix-MAC constructions.~Use `hlextend --help` or the Python library's local API.~For a lab token using SHA-1(secret || message), test candidate secret lengths and append an authorized parameter, then verify against the lab endpoint.~HMAC is not vulnerable to this attack; hash type, padding, and URL encoding must match.

Hydra~Test login credentials against an authorized service using wordlists.~Run `hydra -h` and choose the exact service module and a tiny provided list.~In a local CTF login lab, test two organizer-supplied candidate passwords, then manually verify any reported success.~Failure strings and lockouts can cause false results or disruption; respect rate limits and scope.

iLEAPP (iOS Logs, Events, And Plists Parser)~Parse iOS forensic extractions into artifact reports.~Launch `ileapp` GUI or `ileapp --help` for installed CLI syntax.~Add a supplied iOS extraction, run relevant modules, and inspect a message artifact with its source database path.~iOS versions and encrypted backups affect what is available; verify timestamps and raw source.

ImageMagick~Inspect and transform images from the CLI.~Use `magick identify image.png` and `magick image.png -crop 100x100+0+0 crop.png` (older builds may use `identify`/`convert`).~Crop a tiny QR code from a challenge image and enlarge a copy with nearest-neighbor scaling before ZBar.~Image transformations can alter hidden bits or metadata; keep the original.

Impacket~Python toolkit for network protocols such as SMB/Kerberos in lab environments.~List installed examples and run each script's `-h`; e.g. `GetUserSPNs.py -h`.~In an organizer-provided AD lab, use a read-only enumeration example to list available service principals and verify target/domain credentials.~Examples can authenticate or change remote state; choose only intended lab targets.

innoextract~Extract files from Inno Setup installers without executing them.~Use `innoextract -l installer.exe` and `innoextract -d out installer.exe`.~List a supplied installer, extract its payload, and inspect a bundled config file without running setup.~Not every installer is Inno Setup; extracted scripts/resources may still be active content.

internet_detector~Check whether the environment has internet connectivity.~Run the installed tool's help or documented default check; inspect its local README for flags.~Run it before an offline-only workflow; if it reports connectivity, still follow the contest's network policy and use local data where required.~Connectivity checks may contact external hosts; do not run if the event prohibits such traffic.

IPython~Enhanced interactive Python shell with history and inspection.~Start `ipython`; use `object?` for help and `%run script.py` for a trusted script.~Load `Path('sample.bin').read_bytes()`, inspect slices and hex values interactively, then move the final logic into a reproducible script.~History may retain secrets; interactive state can make results hard to reproduce.

jadx (jadx-gui)~Decompile Android APK/DEX into Java-like source and inspect resources.~Run `jadx-gui app.apk` or `jadx -d out app.apk`.~Open an APK, search for a flag-check method, inspect its string constants, and verify in smali if control flow is ambiguous.~Obfuscation and Kotlin lowering make output approximate; do not run the APK on your main device.

John the Ripper (jumbo)~Audit password hashes and protected-file formats with candidate lists.~Use `john --help`, `john --wordlist=words.txt hashes.txt`, and `john --show hashes.txt`.~Extract a challenge ZIP hash with the appropriate bundled `*2john` helper, test a small list, and validate by opening the archive.~The extraction helper and format must match; a recovered candidate needs verification.

Jpeginfo~Validate JPEG structure and report corruption.~Use `jpeginfo -c image.jpg` and inspect `jpeginfo --help`.~A suspicious JPEG fails structure validation near the end; inspect trailing bytes with xxd/binwalk for appended data.~A clean structure does not rule out steganography; a corrupt structure does not identify the payload.

js-beautify~Format minified JavaScript, HTML, or CSS for reading.~Use `js-beautify min.js -o pretty.js` or the installed CLI variant.~Beautify a supplied script and trace a Base64 constant through a validator.~Formatting does not undo obfuscation or prove runtime behavior; preserve original line offsets.

js-deobfuscator~Attempt automated JavaScript deobfuscation.~Run installed `--help` and supply a copied obfuscated script.~Deobfuscate a string array wrapper, compare a decoded URL with the original code's calls, and test safely.~Different projects use this name; commands and supported patterns vary, and automated output can be incomplete.

jwt_tool~Inspect and test JSON Web Tokens in an authorized web lab.~Run `jwt_tool -h` and provide a supplied token as documented.~Decode a lab JWT, compare header/payload with server behavior, and test only an organizer-intended weakness.~Payload contents are not trusted merely because Base64 decodes; signature validation controls authenticity.

Katana~Crawl authorized web targets and extract discovered URLs.~Run `katana -u http://target/ -d 1` and inspect `-h` for rate/scope controls.~Crawl a local challenge at depth 1, inspect a discovered API path, and verify it manually with curl.~A crawler may follow links outside scope and generate load; constrain domains and depth.

legion~GUI network reconnaissance and service enumeration framework.~Create a project, add only an organizer-provided lab target, and choose a limited scan profile.~Scan a single lab host, inspect an open HTTP service, and verify it with curl or Nmap.~Automated profiles can launch many probes; limit scope and understand each module.

libesedb tools~Inspect Extensible Storage Engine databases such as Windows WebCache.~Use `esedbinfo file.dat` and `esedbexport -t out file.dat` where installed.~Export a supplied WebCache ESE database, locate a URL record, and correlate its timestamp with browser artifacts.~Database files may require related logs for full recovery; exported values need schema interpretation.

LibreOffice~Open office documents, spreadsheets, and presentations.~Open a copy in a restricted environment; inspect sheets, hidden rows/columns, comments, and document properties.~A spreadsheet looks empty until you unhide a sheet containing a challenge clue; verify formulas and raw cell values.~Macros and external links may execute or fetch content; keep them disabled for untrusted files.

lrzip~Decompress large rzip/lrzip archives.~Use `lrzip -t archive.lrz` and `lrzip -d -o output.bin archive.lrz` after checking local help.~Test a supplied LRZ archive, decompress a copy, then inspect the output header with file/xxd.~Decompression can require substantial memory/disk and should not overwrite source.

ltrace~Trace dynamic library calls made by a Linux process.~Run `ltrace ./chall` or `ltrace -e strcmp ./chall`.~Provide a test password and observe a call to `strcmp("AAAA","secret")`; confirm the compared values in gdb or code.~Static linking, direct syscalls, or anti-debugging can prevent useful output; tracing executes code.

lz4~Compress/decompress LZ4 frames.~Use `lz4 -t file.lz4` and `lz4 -d file.lz4 out.bin`.~A challenge file begins with LZ4 frame magic; test it, decompress, and identify the resulting bytes.~Raw LZ4 blocks may lack frame metadata and need known size; extension alone is insufficient.

lzip~Compress/decompress lzip archives.~Use `lzip -t file.lz` and `lzip -d -k file.lz`.~Test a supplied .lz file, decompress while retaining original, and inspect the next container.~Do not confuse .lz (lzip) with .lz4, .lzma, or .lrz.

mac_apt~Parse macOS forensic artifacts and timelines.~Run `mac_apt.py -h` or installed entry point to choose image/input and plugins.~Process a supplied macOS filesystem image with selected plugins, then inspect a Safari/history or user activity CSV.~APFS snapshots, OS versions, and timezones affect results; validate with raw artifacts.

MediaInfo~Report audio/video container, codec, bitrate, frame rate, and tags.~Use `mediainfo media.mp4` or `mediainfo --Output=JSON media.mp4`.~A clip reports two audio streams; extract the unexpected stream with FFmpeg and listen separately.~Metadata can be wrong or spoofed; file container parsing is not proof of visible content.

Metasploit Framework~Framework for lab exploitation, payloads, and auxiliary modules.~Start `msfconsole`; use `search`, `info MODULE`, `show options`, `set RHOSTS`, and `check` where supported.~For an organizer-provided vulnerable service, inspect module requirements, run `check`, then validate the finding manually before any exploit step.~Modules may alter targets or create sessions; only use within explicit competition scope.

mimikatz~Inspect/recover Windows authentication material in authorized memory/lab scenarios.~Use the installed tool's local help and an isolated Windows lab; avoid live systems outside scope.~Given a challenge memory artifact, identify which credential material is present and validate findings with timeline/process context rather than assuming plaintext passwords.~It is highly sensitive and often needs elevation; recovered secrets must not be published.

Miniforge3 (conda)~Manage isolated Python and scientific-computing environments.~Use `conda info`, `conda create -n ctf python=3.11`, and `conda activate ctf`.~Create a case-local environment for a Sage/Python parser and record `conda list` after reproducing the output.~Environment solves/downloads can use network and modify shell config; inspect packages and rules.

multimon-ng~Decode selected radio/audio modulation protocols from audio.~Use `multimon-ng -h`; a common offline form is `multimon-ng -a MODE -t wav signal.wav`.~For a supplied WAV with AFSK1200 tones, enable that decoder and inspect recovered text or packet lines.~Mode and sample format must match; noisy audio creates false decodes.

mupdf-tools (mutool)~Inspect and transform PDF/XPS and related documents from the CLI.~Use `mutool info file.pdf`, `mutool draw -o page-%d.png file.pdf`, and `mutool show file.pdf trailer`.~Render PDF pages to images to inspect a hidden graphic, then use `mutool show` to locate an embedded object referenced by the page.~Rendering may differ from other viewers; preserve the original object structure.

NASM (Netwide Assembler)~Assemble x86/x86-64 assembly into object or flat binary.~Use `nasm -f elf64 test.asm -o test.o` or `nasm -f bin shell.asm -o bytes.bin`.~Assemble a two-instruction test snippet, inspect bytes with xxd, and compare with Ghidra's disassembly.~Output format and bitness must match target; generated bytes can contain relocations in object mode.

Nmap (with Ncat / Nping)~Discover hosts/services; Ncat connects/listens; Nping crafts test probes.~Use `nmap -sV -p 1-1000 TARGET`, `ncat HOST PORT`, and `nping --help`.~Scan one organizer-provided host for the stated ports, connect to a discovered banner with Ncat, and record exact response.~Scans can be noisy or disallowed; restrict hosts, ports, and rate.

Node.js (with npm)~Run JavaScript and manage packages.~Use `node --version`, `node script.js`, `npm --version`, and `npm ci` in a trusted project.~Run a tiny script that decodes `Buffer.from('ZmxhZw==','base64').toString('utf8')` and prints `flag`.~npm install scripts execute code and can use network; inspect package manifests.

obfuscator-io-deobfuscator~Attempt to simplify JavaScript obfuscated by obfuscator.io.~Run installed `--help` and provide a copied JS file as its README describes.~Deobfuscate a string-array wrapper, locate a hidden endpoint, then verify that endpoint is actually used in the original script.~Automated output can be incomplete or behavior-changing; compare with runtime requests.

Obsidian~Organize local Markdown notes with links and search.~Open a case folder as a vault; create notes linking evidence files and tool commands.~Make a note for a packet stream and link it to a recovered file and a hypothesis, then mark whether the hypothesis was verified.~Plugins can execute code or sync data; disable unnecessary plugins for sensitive CTF notes.

oletools (full suite: olevba, oleid, oleobj, rtfobj, mraptor,   msodde, olemeta, oletimes, pyxswf)~Inspect Office/RTF documents for macros, objects, metadata, and suspicious content.~Use `oleid sample.doc`, `olevba sample.doc`, and each tool's `-h`.~Run oleid on a supplied DOC, then olevba to extract VBA; inspect an encoded string and confirm its decode in Python.~Macro indicators are not proof of execution; avoid enabling macros in Office.

OllyDbg~Debug 32-bit Windows executables with a GUI.~Open a copied 32-bit PE in an isolated Windows environment; use breakpoints and step controls.~Break near a password comparison, inspect stack arguments and conditional jump, then test a candidate in the original binary.~OllyDbg is primarily 32-bit and older; modern 64-bit binaries need another debugger.

OpenStego~Hide/extract data in images and support watermarking modes.~Use GUI or `java -jar openstego.jar help`; CLI commands are documented by the installed JAR.~Open a provided stego image, choose Extract Data, supply a known password if given, and inspect extracted bytes.~OpenStego formats need matching mode/password; arbitrary LSB images may not be OpenStego payloads.

padding-oracle-attacker~Automate a CBC padding-oracle test against an explicitly vulnerable lab endpoint.~Read installed README/§--help§ to define ciphertext, oracle request, and valid/invalid response condition.~For a local challenge API returning distinguishable padding errors, confirm one-byte response behavior before asking the tool to recover more bytes.~Many false signals arise from authentication, rate limits, or response parsing; do not use on unrelated services.

PARI/GP~Interactive number theory and algebra system for crypto math.~Start `gp`; use `factor(n)`, `isprime(n)`, `Mod(a,n)^e`, and `lift(...)`.~In a toy RSA challenge with `n=55`, `factor(55)` returns 5 and 11; derive φ=40 and solve for the inverse exponent.~Large secure RSA moduli are not tractable just because a factor command exists; integer types and modulus matter.

PayloadsAllTheThings (offline copy)~Local collection of web/security payload examples and technique notes.~Search its Markdown with `rg -i 'topic' /path/to/PayloadsAllTheThings`.~Find a relevant input-validation example, adapt one harmless test to the lab, and inspect the actual server response.~Examples are context-specific and can be disruptive; validate scope and assumptions.

peda~GDB extension for exploit-development convenience views.~Start GDB after loading peda; use `help peda` or `peda help` depending on installation.~Break at main and inspect peda's register/stack context while the challenge processes input.~Plugin setup varies and can conflict with GEF/pwndbg; use one GDB extension at a time.

peepdf-3~Analyze PDF structure and suspicious objects interactively.~Run `peepdf -h` or open `peepdf -i suspicious.pdf` if supported.~List PDF objects, locate an object containing JavaScript, and inspect its stream bytes before deciding whether it is active.~PDF object references/filters can obscure content; do not assume a suspicious token is executed.

pff-tools (libpff)~Read/export Outlook PST/OST mail stores.~Use `pffinfo mailbox.pst` and `pffexport -t out mailbox.pst` where installed.~Export a supplied PST, inspect a recovered mail attachment and correlate sender/time with headers.~Large stores and partial corruption can omit records; export into an empty directory.

Plaso (log2timeline, psort, pinfo)~Build and query forensic timelines from many artifact sources.~Use `log2timeline.py timeline.plaso image.dd`, `pinfo.py timeline.plaso`, and `psort.py -o l2tcsv timeline.plaso > timeline.csv`.~Create a timeline from a challenge image, filter around a suspicious event time, and corroborate with raw files/EVTX.~Processing can be slow/storage-heavy; timezone and parser version affect output.

pngcheck~Validate PNG chunk structure and CRCs.~Use `pngcheck -v image.png` or `pngcheck -t image.png`.~A copied PNG reports a bad IDAT CRC; locate the chunk offset and compare the bytes in HxD before attempting repair.~A valid PNG can still hide data; a CRC error can be deliberate or accidental.

pwndbg~GDB plugin for exploit and reverse-engineering views.~Start GDB with pwndbg loaded; use `context`, `vmmap`, and `telescope $rsp`.~Break at a crash and inspect stack, mappings, and registers to understand the faulting address.~Plugin command names vary by version; do not load alongside conflicting GDB UI plugins.

pycdc (Decompyle++)~Decompile Python bytecode files to approximate Python source.~Use `pycdc module.pyc > recovered.py` and `pycdas module.pyc` if installed.~Recover a simple Python challenge validator from `.pyc`, then compare decompiled code with disassembly when syntax looks wrong.~Python bytecode versions matter; decompilation can fail or misrepresent control flow.

pyinstxtractor-ng~Extract bundled files from PyInstaller executables.~Use `pyinstxtractor-ng app.exe` or the installed CLI's help syntax.~Extract a PyInstaller challenge PE, locate `.pyc` files, then inspect them with pycdc or uncompyle6.~Extracted bytecode may still be obfuscated; do not run unknown bundled programs.

pypykatz~Parse Windows credential structures from memory/minidumps in authorized forensic labs.~Use `pypykatz -h` and the relevant offline minidump subcommand.~Analyze a supplied LSASS minidump, record any account identifiers, and correlate with the case evidence without exposing secrets.~Results are sensitive and version-dependent; keep dumps and reports private.

Python 2.7~Run legacy scripts that require Python 2 syntax/runtime.~Use `python2 --version` and `python2 legacy.py` only after inspecting the script.~A challenge helper fails on Python 3 because of `print` syntax; run it in Python 2 and compare its output with a manual calculation.~Python 2 is end-of-life; avoid installing untrusted packages or using it for network-facing services.

Python 3.11 (via uv)~Run modern Python scripts and standard-library analysis in a pinned interpreter.~Use `uv python list`, `uv run --python 3.11 script.py`, or `uv venv --python 3.11 .venv`.~Decode a hex challenge string with `python -c "print(bytes.fromhex('666c6167'))"` in the uv-managed environment; output is `b'flag'`.~Quote shell commands carefully; distinguish bytes from Unicode and record package versions.

qemu-img (qemu-utils)~Inspect and convert virtual disk image formats without booting them.~Use `qemu-img info disk.qcow2` and `qemu-img convert -O raw disk.qcow2 disk.raw`.~Convert a supplied QCOW2 copy to raw, then analyze partitions with The Sleuth Kit.~Conversion needs free disk space; backing files/snapshots may be required for a complete image.

radare2~CLI reverse-engineering suite for disassembly, analysis, and patching copies.~Use `r2 -A binary`; inside, `afl` lists functions, `iz` strings, `pdf @ main` disassembles, `q` quits.~Find a “Correct” string in `iz`, follow its references, and inspect the surrounding branch.~Analysis heuristics and decompiler plugins vary; commands can modify files in write mode.

rat-king-parser~Parse configuration data from supported remote-access malware families for analysis.~Read local README and invoke its supported sample input on a copied binary.~Run it on a known supported CTF sample, extract a candidate C2 host/config field, then confirm the bytes in the binary.~It supports particular families/versions, not arbitrary RATs; configuration may be encrypted or absent.

RegRipper~Extract Windows Registry artifact reports through plugins.~Use `rip.pl -r NTUSER.DAT -p userassist` or `rip.pl -r SYSTEM -f system` with installed plugin names.~Parse a copied NTUSER.DAT, inspect UserAssist entries, and correlate candidate program activity with Prefetch.~Plugin output needs OS/version context; Registry LastWrite time is not always action time.

ripgrep (rg)~Fast recursive text search with regex and file filters.~Use `rg -n -i 'flag|secret' folder`, `rg --files folder`, and `rg -g '*.py' 'password' .`.~Search extracted source for a validation string, then open the exact reported file and line to trace code.~Binary files and hidden files may be skipped by default; add options when needed.

rockyou.txt (Kali 'wordlists' package)~Common password wordlist for offline candidate testing.~Locate the file, often `/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz`, and decompress a working copy with gzip if needed.~Use a small relevant subset against a provided challenge hash with John/hashcat, then verify any recovered candidate.~Large generic lists waste time; wordlists contain sensitive/common passwords and are not proof of a hash type.

ROPgadget~Search binaries for return-oriented programming instruction sequences.~Use `ROPgadget --binary ./chall` and inspect `--help` for filtering.~Find a `pop rdi; ret` gadget in a lab ELF, then confirm its address and bytes in objdump/Ghidra.~Reported gadgets depend on architecture/offsets and may be unusable under PIE/ASLR or constraints.

rtptools (rtpdump, rtpplay and others)~Inspect, replay, or manipulate RTP packet streams for media forensics.~Use `rtpdump -h` and select the installed command matching the capture format.~Extract an RTP stream from a supplied PCAP, reconstruct its payload, and compare audio timing with Wireshark stream analysis.~RTP codecs and sequence loss affect playback; do not replay onto real networks without authorization.

Rust (rustup, rustc, cargo)~Compile/run Rust helpers and manage toolchains.~Use `rustc --version`, `cargo new demo`, `cargo run`, and `cargo build --release`.~Write a byte parser in Rust for a custom record, compile, then compare parsed integers with xxd/Python.~Cargo builds can fetch dependencies and execute build scripts; inspect `Cargo.toml` and source.

rustscan~Fast port discovery frontend often paired with Nmap.~Use `rustscan -a TARGET -- -sV` and check `--help` for rate/batch limits.~Scan one organizer-provided lab host, note open ports, and verify services with Nmap/curl.~High-speed scanning can overload targets; restrict rate, scope, and ports.

SageMath~Computer algebra system for crypto and number theory.~Start `sage` or run `sage solve.sage`; use `factor`, modular rings, matrices, and polynomial methods.~For toy RSA `n=55`, factor it and compute `inverse_mod(3,40)` to get a private exponent 27; verify `(m^3)^27 mod 55 == m` for valid messages.~Mathematical assumptions matter; Sage syntax and integer/ring types can change results.

SecLists~Collection of wordlists for discovery, fuzzing, and testing.~Locate `/usr/share/seclists` and choose a short list appropriate to the target.~Use a small web-content list with ffuf against an authorized local site, then verify a discovered path manually.~Large lists create excessive traffic and false leads; select by task and rate limit.

socat~Relay data between sockets, files, and terminals.~Use `socat -h`; e.g. `socat - TCP:127.0.0.1:9000` to interact with a lab service.~Connect to an organizer-provided TCP challenge and observe its prompt, then send test input from the terminal.~Bidirectional relays can hang or expose listeners; bind only to intended interfaces.

Sonic Visualiser~View audio waveforms, spectrograms, and frequency features.~Open a WAV and add a spectrogram layer; zoom to suspect time/frequency.~A challenge WAV displays a narrow-band pattern spelling digits in the spectrogram; note the time span and confirm with Audacity/SoX.~Display settings can hide faint signals; spectral patterns may be incidental.

SoX (Sound eXchange)~Inspect, convert, trim, reverse, and analyze audio from the CLI.~Use `soxi audio.wav`, `sox audio.wav trimmed.wav trim 5 10`, and `sox audio.wav -n spectrogram -o spec.png`.~Create a spectrogram from a supplied WAV, see DTMF-like tones, then decode with a suitable allowed tool or manual frequency check.~Resampling and compression can remove clues; use copies and record parameters.

SQLCipher Community Edition — CLI~Open SQLite databases encrypted with SQLCipher when the key is known or recovered.~Use `sqlcipher encrypted.db`, then `PRAGMA key='known-key';` and `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master;`.~With a supplied key, open an encrypted app database and query a message table; verify decryption by a sane schema.~Wrong key often appears as “file is not a database”; cipher compatibility/settings can differ.

sqlite3~Query and inspect SQLite databases from the terminal.~Use `sqlite3 database.db`; inside `.tables`, `.schema`, and `SELECT * FROM table LIMIT 10;`.~Open a copied chat database, inspect schema, then select messages in timestamp order and verify source row IDs.~Copy WAL/SHM files too when present; opening databases may create journal files.

sqlmap~Test SQL injection in explicitly authorized web challenges.~Use `sqlmap -u 'http://lab/item?id=1' -p id --batch` only within scope; inspect `-h` for risk/level options.~On a local vulnerable training page, confirm a parameter behaves differently under a simple manual test, then let sqlmap test that one parameter and inspect its evidence.~It can generate heavy traffic and modify data depending on options; constrain target and avoid destructive flags.

sstv (command-line SSTV decoder)~Decode slow-scan television images from audio recordings.~Run `sstv --help` and supply a copied WAV in the format the installed decoder expects.~Decode a supplied SSTV WAV into an image, then inspect its text or QR code with image tools.~Modes and sample rate matter; a failed decode can mean wrong mode or noisy audio.

steghide~Embed/extract data in supported JPEG/BMP/WAV/AU carriers using a passphrase.~Use `steghide info image.jpg` and `steghide extract -sf image.jpg -xf payload.bin`.~Given an organizer-supplied passphrase, extract a payload from a JPEG and inspect its file signature.~Wrong passphrases and unsupported carriers produce failures; steghide does not detect every stego scheme.

stegseek~Test passphrase candidates for steghide payloads using a wordlist.~Use `stegseek image.jpg words.txt` and inspect `--help` for output options.~On a challenge JPEG known to contain steghide data, use a short clue-based list and verify the extracted file.~It targets steghide format specifically; a failed wordlist does not prove no payload.

stegsnow (SNOW)~Hide/recover data in trailing spaces and tabs of text files.~Use `stegsnow -h`; extraction commonly uses `stegsnow file.txt` or `stegsnow -C -p PASSWORD file.txt`.~A supplied text file looks normal, but SNOW extracts a short message from line-end whitespace; compare raw bytes before editing.~Editors may strip trailing whitespace; preserve the original file exactly.

StegSolve~GUI tool for image bit planes, color channels, and frame comparisons.~Launch its Java JAR, load a copied image, then cycle bit-plane views.~Inspect a PNG's red-channel LSB plane and see a high-contrast message invisible in the normal view.~Visual patterns are clues; export the plane and confirm actual bytes if possible.

strace~Trace Linux system calls made by a process.~Run `strace -o trace.txt ./chall` or `strace -e openat,read,write ./chall`.~Run a challenge executable and see it attempts to open `secret.txt`; provide a controlled test file and observe changed behavior.~Tracing executes code and may perturb timing; filtered traces can omit relevant syscalls.

Subfinder~Enumerate subdomains from passive sources for authorized domains.~Use `subfinder -d example.test` and inspect `-h` for offline/source settings.~For an organizer-authorized domain, collect candidate subdomains and verify only those in scope.~It usually queries external services, so an offline-only event may make it unusable; passive results can be stale.

Sublime Text~Fast GUI editor for source and large text files.~Open a copied source tree; use Find in Files and syntax highlighting.~Search extracted JavaScript for `atob(`, inspect the surrounding function, and record the exact file/line.~Editing can alter line endings/encoding; do not save forensic originals.

tar~Create/list/extract tar archives.~Use `tar -tf archive.tar` to list and `tar -xf archive.tar -C out` to extract.~List a challenge TAR before extraction, then inspect a nested `notes.txt` in an empty output directory.~Archives may contain absolute paths, symlinks, or traversal entries; inspect names before extraction.

tcpdump~Capture and inspect packets from an interface or PCAP.~Use `tcpdump -nn -r capture.pcap` and `tcpdump -i IFACE -w capture.pcap` for authorized capture.~Read a supplied PCAP with `tcpdump -nn -r`, filter `host 10.0.0.5 and port 80`, then pivot to Wireshark for stream reconstruction.~Capture filters use BPF syntax and can omit packets permanently; live capture may need privileges.

TestDisk and PhotoRec~Recover partitions/filesystem metadata (TestDisk) and carve files by signatures (PhotoRec).~Start `testdisk image.dd` or `photorec image.dd` and follow GUI menus on a copy.~Use TestDisk to inspect a missing FAT partition; if metadata is gone, use PhotoRec to carve JPEGs into a separate folder.~Recovery can be partial; PhotoRec usually loses filenames/paths. Never write recovered data onto source media.

unar~Extract archives in many formats with automatic text encoding detection.~Use `lsar archive` to list and `unar -o out archive` to extract.~List an old archive with non-ASCII filenames, extract it, and inspect the recovered file names/content.~Some archives have duplicate paths or encrypted entries; use an empty destination.

uncompyle6~Decompile supported Python bytecode versions to Python-like source.~Use `uncompyle6 -o out module.pyc` and check version support with `--help`.~Decompile a supplied Python 3.7 pyc validator, inspect its condition, and compare with a bytecode disassembler if output looks odd.~Not all Python versions are supported; decompiled source may differ semantically at edge cases.

unpyc3 (unpyc37-3.10)~Decompile certain Python 3.7–3.10 bytecode variants.~Run the installed entry point's `--help` and pass a copied `.pyc` file.~Use it when uncompyle6 cannot handle a supplied pyc; compare recovered condition with pycdc output.~Exact supported versions and CLI name vary by package; never assume recovered code is exact.

unrar~List/test/extract RAR archives.~Use `unrar l archive.rar`, `unrar t archive.rar`, and `unrar x archive.rar out/`.~List an archive, test its integrity, extract a supplied encrypted member using the known clue password, and inspect it.~RAR format versions and password protection vary; extract into a dedicated directory.

unzip~List/test/extract ZIP archives.~Use `unzip -l archive.zip`, `unzip -t archive.zip`, and `unzip archive.zip -d out`.~List and test a challenge ZIP, then extract an inner text file into a fresh folder.~ZIP paths and symlinks can be unsafe; inspect names and avoid overwriting existing files.

UPX~Pack/unpack executables using UPX format.~Use `upx -t sample.exe` to test and `upx -d -o unpacked.exe sample.exe` to unpack a copy.~DIE suggests UPX, UPX test passes, and the unpacked executable exposes readable strings for Ghidra.~Not all packers are UPX; a modified header can defeat normal unpacking, and unpacked code is still untrusted.

Visual Studio Code~Edit, search, and debug source files in a project.~Open a copied challenge folder, use global search, then inspect source and debugger configuration.~Search a provided Python project for `verify`, set a breakpoint in the validator, and run a trusted test input.~Workspace tasks/extensions can execute code; inspect settings before trusting a downloaded project.

Volatility 2~Analyze memory images with the older Volatility 2 plugin/profile model.~Run `vol.py -f memory.raw imageinfo`, then `vol.py -f memory.raw --profile=PROFILE pslist` when applicable.~Identify a Windows memory image profile, enumerate processes, then use cmdline/netscan-style plugins appropriate to that profile.~Volatility 2 syntax differs from 3 and relies on exact profiles; old builds may require Python 2.

Volatility 2 community plugins~Extend Volatility 2 with third-party memory-analysis plugins.~Use `vol.py --plugins=/path/to/plugins --info` to list compatible additions.~Load a supplied plugin, confirm it appears in `--info`, run it on a copied memory image, and verify any hit with core plugins.~Third-party code executes in your analysis environment and may target narrow versions; inspect source.

Volatility 2 profiles (Linux and macOS)~Provide symbols/types required for Volatility 2 Linux/macOS images.~Place the matching profile ZIP in the configured profile directory and inspect `vol.py --info`.~A Linux memory image fails without symbols; add the exact kernel-build profile and rerun `linux_pslist`.~A profile from a similar but different kernel can yield wrong or empty results.

Volatility 3 community plugins (community3)~Add third-party plugins to Volatility 3.~Use `vol -p /path/to/community3 -h` to list plugins, plus symbols if required.~Run an added artifact plugin on a supplied memory image and corroborate its output with core Volatility plugins.~Plugin API compatibility changes; third-party code executes locally, so inspect source and version.

VS Code extension: C/C++ (ms-vscode.cpptools)~Provide C/C++ language navigation and debugging in VS Code.~Open a C/C++ project and configure include paths/compiler and a launch configuration.~Set a breakpoint in a trusted C validator, debug with a sample input, and inspect variables beside the source.~IntelliSense is not the compiler; debug configs can execute builds and targets.

VS Code extension: Python (ms-python.python)~Provide Python interpreter selection, linting, and debugging in VS Code.~Select the uv/venv interpreter and create a Python launch configuration.~Set a breakpoint inside a decoder loop, run a test byte string, and inspect intermediate bytes.~The selected interpreter may differ from terminal Python; check version and environment.

YARA~Match files against rules describing byte/text patterns and conditions.~Use `yara rule.yar sample.bin` and `yara -r rule.yar folder`.~Write a rule matching an exact challenge marker and a PE header condition, run it on supplied files, then inspect matched bytes in HxD.~A rule match means its condition was true, not that a file is malicious; broad rules produce false positives.

yara-python (and YARA on Linux)~Apply YARA rules from Python or the Linux CLI.~Use `yara.compile(filepath='rule.yar').match('sample.bin')` in Python or `yara rule.yar sample.bin`.~Compile a rule matching a known 4-byte signature, scan a case directory, and print match filenames for manual validation.~Rules are user-supplied code-like patterns; API details and match object fields vary by version.

zip~Create and update ZIP archives.~Use `zip output.zip file.txt` and `zip -r output.zip folder/`; use unzip to inspect.~Package extracted challenge artifacts for local organization, then `unzip -t output.zip` to verify integrity.~ZIP password options often use weak ZipCrypto; do not rely on them for confidentiality.

zstd~Compress/decompress Zstandard streams.~Use `zstd -t file.zst`, `zstd -d -k file.zst`, and `zstd -dc file.zst > out.bin`.~A file begins Zstandard magic `28 B5 2F FD`; test, decompress, then identify the next layer.~Frames can be concatenated; decompressed output may be much larger than input.

Zui (formerly Brim)~GUI exploration of structured logs and packet-derived data using Zed queries.~Open a PCAP or Zed data pool, then filter events by service, IP, or field.~Import a challenge PCAP, find DNS events for a rare domain, then inspect the exact packets in Wireshark/TShark.~Schema and query syntax differ from SQL; imported data may be summarized rather than full raw packets.
